Empirical Research Plan: “How Do Social Norms Affect the Pricing and Performance of ‘Sin’ Stocks?”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Chosen design: Difference-in-Differences (DID) in a two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) panel, complemented by an event-study dynamic specification.

Why DID?  
• We observe firms repeatedly over 1965-2006.  
• Social norms vary exogenously across space (religiosity of the firm’s headquarters state) and time (long-run secular decline in church attendance, evangelical revivals of the late 1970s/early-1980s, etc.).  
• “Sin” status itself is time-invariant, but the intensity of the social stigma is plausibly stronger in high-religiosity areas and when religiosity rises.  
• By interacting a time-varying measure of local religiosity with a time-invariant Sin indicator, we obtain quasi-experimental variation: a treated group (sin firms exposed to high religiosity) and several comparison groups (sin firms in low-religiosity areas and all non-sin firms).

Formally:

Return_it  = β ( Sin_i × HighReligiosity_st ) + γ_i + δ_t + X_itθ + ε_it

where s indexes the state of headquarters, i the firm, t the year.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Treatment variable: Sin_i × HighReligiosity_st  
  – Sin_i = 1 for firms in SIC codes for alcohol (2080–2086), tobacco (2100–2199), and gaming (7990–7999).  
  – HighReligiosity_st = 1 if state-year religious adherence rate (ARDA; % of population in religious congregations) is above the yearly national median.

• Control groups:  
  1. Sin firms in low-religiosity states (difference across space).  
  2. Non-sin firms in both high- and low-religiosity states (difference across industry).  
  These comparisons are folded into the interaction term and captured via firm and year FE.

• Treatment timing: continuously varying by year; firms “enter treatment” whenever HighReligiosity_st = 1. The event-study version uses the first switch from 0→1 for each state.

No running variable / cutoff (not an RDD).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends: Absent religiosity, sin and non-sin firms would have followed the same trend in returns within a state.  
‒ Plausibility: Within-state secular economic shocks hit both groups; firm and year FE absorb constant differences and macro shocks. We will test pre-trends graphically.

A2. Exogeneity of religiosity shocks: Short-run changes in religiosity are orthogonal to unobserved determinants of firm performance.  
‒ Plausibility: Demographic shifts in religiosity largely driven by migration and national movements, unlikely linked to firm-level fundamentals.

A3. Stable composition: Firms do not systematically move HQs in anticipation of religiosity or re-classify as “sin.”  
‒ Plausibility: HQ relocation is rare and will be checked; “sin” SIC codes are technologically determined.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Omitted local economic conditions correlated with religiosity (e.g., Bible-belt economic decline).  
   ⇒ Add state×year economic controls (unemployment, income growth), industry×year FE, and state-specific trends.

T2. Selection of firms into (or out of) high-religiosity states.  
   ⇒ Drop observations where the firm changes headquarters; robustness: include firm×state fixed effects or instrument HighReligiosity with lagged county-level religious revivals.

T3. Measurement error in religiosity data.  
   ⇒ Use multiple sources (ARDA, General Social Survey) and a continuous measure; show robustness to alternative cutoffs (top tercile, z-scored).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# ------------------------------------------------------
# 0) Packages
# ------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)

# ------------------------------------------------------
# 1) Load data
# ------------------------------------------------------
stocks   <- fread("sin_stocks_1965_2006.csv")      # firm-year panel
religion <- fread("state_religiosity_1965_2006.csv") # state-year panel

# ------------------------------------------------------
# 2) Merge & variable construction
# ------------------------------------------------------
DT <- merge(stocks, religion, by = c("state","year"))
DT[, sin := as.integer(sic %in% c(2080:2086,2100:2199,7990:7999))]
DT[, high_rel := as.integer(rel_rate > median(rel_rate)), by = year]
DT[, treat  := sin * high_rel]

# Control variables
DT[, ln_mcap  := log(market_cap)]
DT[, bm_ratio := book_equity / market_cap]

# ------------------------------------------------------
# 3) Main TWFE DID regression
# ------------------------------------------------------
fe_eq <- feols(ret_excess ~ treat + ln_mcap + bm_ratio | gvkey + year,
               data = DT, cluster = ~state)

summary(fe_eq)

# ------------------------------------------------------
# 4) Event-study (pre-trend test)
# ------------------------------------------------------
# First year a state crosses above median
religion[, first_high := year[ which(high_rel==1)[1] ], by = state]
DT <- merge(DT, religion[, .(state, year, first_high)], by = c("state","year"))
DT[, rel_time := year - first_high]
DT <- DT[rel_time >= -5 & rel_time <= 5]            # window

ev_eq <- feols(ret_excess ~ i(rel_time, sin, ref=-1) + ln_mcap + bm_ratio |
               gvkey + year, data = DT, cluster = ~state)
iplot(ev_eq)   # fixest built-in plot

# ------------------------------------------------------
# 5) Robustness: alternative cutoff (top tercile)
# ------------------------------------------------------
DT[, high_rel3 := as.integer(rel_rate > quantile(rel_rate, .66)), by = year]
DT[, treat3    := sin * high_rel3]

robust_eq <- feols(ret_excess ~ treat3 + ln_mcap + bm_ratio |
                   gvkey + year, data = DT, cluster = ~state)
summary(robust_eq)
```

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Economic theory (under‐pricing of firms shunned by certain investors) predicts:
β < 0 for valuation multiples (sin stocks cheaper)  
β > 0 for subsequent average returns (investors require higher expected return)

Magnitude prior: A 3–5 percentage-point higher annual excess return for treated sin firms (≈40–70 bps monthly), echoing standard factor premia.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Pre-treatment trends visually parallel …… 0.8  
C2: No simultaneous confounders ………………… 0.6  
C3: No endogenous sorting into treatment …… 0.7  
C4: No spillovers / interference ………………… 0.9  
C5: Correct inference (clustered SEs) ………… 1.0  
Overall (average) ………………………………………… 0.8

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
End of Plan
